case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s undergoing peritoneal dialysis for kidney failure who was also being investigated for severe hyperparathyroidism presented with multiple skin lesions 1 day after undergoing cervical computed tomography with iodinated contrast. Physical examination revealed a polymorphous cutaneous eruption characterized by nodular vegetating lesions on the lower lip and right nasal ala (Figure 1A); papulovesicular lesions, either umbilicated or with an erosive center, clustered on the left cheek (Figure 1B); and 2 papulovesicular lesions with an erythematous-to-violaceous halo at the cannula insertion sites on the back of the right hand and the inner side of the wrist. The patient reported that the lesions were painful, with the ones in the oral mucosa impairing feeding. Additional symptoms included fever, fatigue, rhinorrhea, and odynophagia. Investigations revealed a negative COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction test, mildly raised inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 24.2 mg/dL), normal thyroid function test results, and a negative virology screen, including both polymerase chain reaction and IgM tests for herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2, varicella-zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus.
case_info.caption: Nodular vegetating lesions on the chin, lower lip, and right nasal ala (A), and papulovesicular lesions on the left hemiface (B).
case_info.explanation: Cutaneous biopsies of the vegetating lesion on the lip and 1 of the hand lesions showed a dense neutrophilic infiltrate on the reticular dermis with multiple foci of vasculitis, including marked fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls (Figure 2A). Multiple round mononucleated cells with an optically empty peripheral perinuclear halo were also identified (Figure 2B). Immunohistochemistry findings revealed diffuse positivity for myeloperoxidase that spared the round cells, which positive for the histiocytic marker CD163 and, focally, for CD3; CD20 was negative. Results of Ziehl-Neelsen and periodic acid–Schiff stains ruled out the presence of microorganisms. Clinical and pathological findings were in keeping with iododerma. The diagnosis was corroborated by a markedly raised serum iodine level (19 992 μg/L [normal range, 45-100 μg/L]). Complete resolution of skin lesions was possible with a combination of topical fusidic acid with betamethasone and oral corticosteroid 0.5 mg/kg/d tapered over 1 month. The patient’s fatigue and malaise also considerably improved. Iododerma is a rare type of halogenoderma that develops after exposure to iodine-containing compounds (eg, oral and intravenous iodinated contrast dyes, potassium iodide, amiodarone, topical wound care products). It mainly affects patients with kidney disease owing to impaired renal clearance and accumulation of iodine in the bloodstream.1,2Generally, it takes months of continuous exposure to a halogen (eg, oral iodine) to develop a halogenoderma. However, in the context of intravenous administration, cutaneous lesions can appear within 2 to 3 days (ranging from several hours to 8 days), especially in the context of kidney failure.1-3 Iododerma can present a diagnostic challenge. Clinically, lesions can progress rapidly and be polymorphous. However, the most common presentations are acneiform pustular eruptions1and vegetative plaques.2,4In extreme cases, patients can experience toxic effects and present with multiorgan involvement.2 Pathologically, a neutrophil-predominant inflammatory infiltrate is fairly unspecific and can be found in neutrophilic dermatoses such as Sweet syndrome and some infectious diseases.5In the present case, we also found histologic features that had recently been described in iododerma, namely a neutrophilic dermatosis with vasculitis and haloed structures simulatingCryptococcus.2Similarly to the 3 cases previously reported by Ko et al,5we showed that these cryptococcal-like structures were positive for a histiocytic marker and negative for myeloperoxidase. These structures in the setting of neutrophilic dermatosis should also be recognized as part of the histologic spectrum of iododerma. Knowledge of this histologic mimicker is important not only to facilitate the diagnosis, but also to avoid unnecessary antifungal medications.6 Pemphigus vegetans is a rare variant of pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid blisters that become erosions and can form fungoid vegetations in intertriginous areas, the face, and scalp. The characteristic tongue involvement and the presence of suprabasal acantholysis with positive immunofluorescence are distinct aspects.7Pyostomatitis vegetans is characterized by oral involvement with classic snail-track erosions, a strong association with inflammatory bowel disease, peripheral eosinophilia, and characteristic histological features (eg, intraepithelial abscesses with large amount of eosinophils).8Superficial granulomatous pyoderma is a rare variant of pyoderma gangrenosum with a more indolent course. However, facial involvement is particularly uncommon. A characteristic 3-layered granuloma is seen on histological findings.9 With the present case we want to highlight that, despite the diagnostic challenges, a history of exposure to iodine in the context of kidney disease with acute acneiform and/or vegetating lesions should raise the suspicion of iododerma. The diagnosis can be reiterated by histological findings of neutrophilic dermatosis with cryptococcal-like structures (with or without vasculitis), and confirmed by high serum or urine iodine levels. The main treatment of iododerma is to remove the trigger. In some cases, no additional therapy is required. In the case reported, the lesions healed completely with use of systemic corticosteroids, but cyclosporine and hemodialysis are possible alternatives.4

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s undergoing peritoneal dialysis for kidney failure who was also being investigated for severe hyperparathyroidism presented with multiple skin lesions 1 day after undergoing cervical computed tomography with iodinated contrast. Physical examination revealed a polymorphous cutaneous eruption characterized by nodular vegetating lesions on the lower lip and right nasal ala (Figure 1A); papulovesicular lesions, either umbilicated or with an erosive center, clustered on the left cheek (Figure 1B); and 2 papulovesicular lesions with an erythematous-to-violaceous halo at the cannula insertion sites on the back of the right hand and the inner side of the wrist. The patient reported that the lesions were painful, with the ones in the oral mucosa impairing feeding. Additional symptoms included fever, fatigue, rhinorrhea, and odynophagia. Investigations revealed a negative COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction test, mildly raised inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 24.2 mg/dL), normal thyroid function test results, and a negative virology screen, including both polymerase chain reaction and IgM tests for herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2, varicella-zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus.
case_info.caption: Nodular vegetating lesions on the chin, lower lip, and right nasal ala (A), and papulovesicular lesions on the left hemiface (B).
case_info.explanation: Cutaneous biopsies of the vegetating lesion on the lip and 1 of the hand lesions showed a dense neutrophilic infiltrate on the reticular dermis with multiple foci of vasculitis, including marked fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls (Figure 2A). Multiple round mononucleated cells with an optically empty peripheral perinuclear halo were also identified (Figure 2B). Immunohistochemistry findings revealed diffuse positivity for myeloperoxidase that spared the round cells, which positive for the histiocytic marker CD163 and, focally, for CD3; CD20 was negative. Results of Ziehl-Neelsen and periodic acid–Schiff stains ruled out the presence of microorganisms. Clinical and pathological findings were in keeping with iododerma. The diagnosis was corroborated by a markedly raised serum iodine level (19 992 μg/L [normal range, 45-100 μg/L]). Complete resolution of skin lesions was possible with a combination of topical fusidic acid with betamethasone and oral corticosteroid 0.5 mg/kg/d tapered over 1 month. The patient’s fatigue and malaise also considerably improved. Iododerma is a rare type of halogenoderma that develops after exposure to iodine-containing compounds (eg, oral and intravenous iodinated contrast dyes, potassium iodide, amiodarone, topical wound care products). It mainly affects patients with kidney disease owing to impaired renal clearance and accumulation of iodine in the bloodstream.1,2Generally, it takes months of continuous exposure to a halogen (eg, oral iodine) to develop a halogenoderma. However, in the context of intravenous administration, cutaneous lesions can appear within 2 to 3 days (ranging from several hours to 8 days), especially in the context of kidney failure.1-3 Iododerma can present a diagnostic challenge. Clinically, lesions can progress rapidly and be polymorphous. However, the most common presentations are acneiform pustular eruptions1and vegetative plaques.2,4In extreme cases, patients can experience toxic effects and present with multiorgan involvement.2 Pathologically, a neutrophil-predominant inflammatory infiltrate is fairly unspecific and can be found in neutrophilic dermatoses such as Sweet syndrome and some infectious diseases.5In the present case, we also found histologic features that had recently been described in iododerma, namely a neutrophilic dermatosis with vasculitis and haloed structures simulatingCryptococcus.2Similarly to the 3 cases previously reported by Ko et al,5we showed that these cryptococcal-like structures were positive for a histiocytic marker and negative for myeloperoxidase. These structures in the setting of neutrophilic dermatosis should also be recognized as part of the histologic spectrum of iododerma. Knowledge of this histologic mimicker is important not only to facilitate the diagnosis, but also to avoid unnecessary antifungal medications.6 Pemphigus vegetans is a rare variant of pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid blisters that become erosions and can form fungoid vegetations in intertriginous areas, the face, and scalp. The characteristic tongue involvement and the presence of suprabasal acantholysis with positive immunofluorescence are distinct aspects.7Pyostomatitis vegetans is characterized by oral involvement with classic snail-track erosions, a strong association with inflammatory bowel disease, peripheral eosinophilia, and characteristic histological features (eg, intraepithelial abscesses with large amount of eosinophils).8Superficial granulomatous pyoderma is a rare variant of pyoderma gangrenosum with a more indolent course. However, facial involvement is particularly uncommon. A characteristic 3-layered granuloma is seen on histological findings.9 With the present case we want to highlight that, despite the diagnostic challenges, a history of exposure to iodine in the context of kidney disease with acute acneiform and/or vegetating lesions should raise the suspicion of iododerma. The diagnosis can be reiterated by histological findings of neutrophilic dermatosis with cryptococcal-like structures (with or without vasculitis), and confirmed by high serum or urine iodine levels. The main treatment of iododerma is to remove the trigger. In some cases, no additional therapy is required. In the case reported, the lesions healed completely with use of systemic corticosteroids, but cyclosporine and hemodialysis are possible alternatives.4

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s undergoing peritoneal dialysis for kidney failure who was also being investigated for severe hyperparathyroidism presented with multiple skin lesions 1 day after undergoing cervical computed tomography with iodinated contrast. Physical examination revealed a polymorphous cutaneous eruption characterized by nodular vegetating lesions on the lower lip and right nasal ala (Figure 1A); papulovesicular lesions, either umbilicated or with an erosive center, clustered on the left cheek (Figure 1B); and 2 papulovesicular lesions with an erythematous-to-violaceous halo at the cannula insertion sites on the back of the right hand and the inner side of the wrist. The patient reported that the lesions were painful, with the ones in the oral mucosa impairing feeding. Additional symptoms included fever, fatigue, rhinorrhea, and odynophagia. Investigations revealed a negative COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction test, mildly raised inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 24.2 mg/dL), normal thyroid function test results, and a negative virology screen, including both polymerase chain reaction and IgM tests for herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2, varicella-zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus.
case_info.caption: Nodular vegetating lesions on the chin, lower lip, and right nasal ala (A), and papulovesicular lesions on the left hemiface (B).
case_info.explanation: Cutaneous biopsies of the vegetating lesion on the lip and 1 of the hand lesions showed a dense neutrophilic infiltrate on the reticular dermis with multiple foci of vasculitis, including marked fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls (Figure 2A). Multiple round mononucleated cells with an optically empty peripheral perinuclear halo were also identified (Figure 2B). Immunohistochemistry findings revealed diffuse positivity for myeloperoxidase that spared the round cells, which positive for the histiocytic marker CD163 and, focally, for CD3; CD20 was negative. Results of Ziehl-Neelsen and periodic acid–Schiff stains ruled out the presence of microorganisms. Clinical and pathological findings were in keeping with iododerma. The diagnosis was corroborated by a markedly raised serum iodine level (19 992 μg/L [normal range, 45-100 μg/L]). Complete resolution of skin lesions was possible with a combination of topical fusidic acid with betamethasone and oral corticosteroid 0.5 mg/kg/d tapered over 1 month. The patient’s fatigue and malaise also considerably improved. Iododerma is a rare type of halogenoderma that develops after exposure to iodine-containing compounds (eg, oral and intravenous iodinated contrast dyes, potassium iodide, amiodarone, topical wound care products). It mainly affects patients with kidney disease owing to impaired renal clearance and accumulation of iodine in the bloodstream.1,2Generally, it takes months of continuous exposure to a halogen (eg, oral iodine) to develop a halogenoderma. However, in the context of intravenous administration, cutaneous lesions can appear within 2 to 3 days (ranging from several hours to 8 days), especially in the context of kidney failure.1-3 Iododerma can present a diagnostic challenge. Clinically, lesions can progress rapidly and be polymorphous. However, the most common presentations are acneiform pustular eruptions1and vegetative plaques.2,4In extreme cases, patients can experience toxic effects and present with multiorgan involvement.2 Pathologically, a neutrophil-predominant inflammatory infiltrate is fairly unspecific and can be found in neutrophilic dermatoses such as Sweet syndrome and some infectious diseases.5In the present case, we also found histologic features that had recently been described in iododerma, namely a neutrophilic dermatosis with vasculitis and haloed structures simulatingCryptococcus.2Similarly to the 3 cases previously reported by Ko et al,5we showed that these cryptococcal-like structures were positive for a histiocytic marker and negative for myeloperoxidase. These structures in the setting of neutrophilic dermatosis should also be recognized as part of the histologic spectrum of iododerma. Knowledge of this histologic mimicker is important not only to facilitate the diagnosis, but also to avoid unnecessary antifungal medications.6 Pemphigus vegetans is a rare variant of pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid blisters that become erosions and can form fungoid vegetations in intertriginous areas, the face, and scalp. The characteristic tongue involvement and the presence of suprabasal acantholysis with positive immunofluorescence are distinct aspects.7Pyostomatitis vegetans is characterized by oral involvement with classic snail-track erosions, a strong association with inflammatory bowel disease, peripheral eosinophilia, and characteristic histological features (eg, intraepithelial abscesses with large amount of eosinophils).8Superficial granulomatous pyoderma is a rare variant of pyoderma gangrenosum with a more indolent course. However, facial involvement is particularly uncommon. A characteristic 3-layered granuloma is seen on histological findings.9 With the present case we want to highlight that, despite the diagnostic challenges, a history of exposure to iodine in the context of kidney disease with acute acneiform and/or vegetating lesions should raise the suspicion of iododerma. The diagnosis can be reiterated by histological findings of neutrophilic dermatosis with cryptococcal-like structures (with or without vasculitis), and confirmed by high serum or urine iodine levels. The main treatment of iododerma is to remove the trigger. In some cases, no additional therapy is required. In the case reported, the lesions healed completely with use of systemic corticosteroids, but cyclosporine and hemodialysis are possible alternatives.4

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s undergoing peritoneal dialysis for kidney failure who was also being investigated for severe hyperparathyroidism presented with multiple skin lesions 1 day after undergoing cervical computed tomography with iodinated contrast. Physical examination revealed a polymorphous cutaneous eruption characterized by nodular vegetating lesions on the lower lip and right nasal ala (Figure 1A); papulovesicular lesions, either umbilicated or with an erosive center, clustered on the left cheek (Figure 1B); and 2 papulovesicular lesions with an erythematous-to-violaceous halo at the cannula insertion sites on the back of the right hand and the inner side of the wrist. The patient reported that the lesions were painful, with the ones in the oral mucosa impairing feeding. Additional symptoms included fever, fatigue, rhinorrhea, and odynophagia. Investigations revealed a negative COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction test, mildly raised inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 24.2 mg/dL), normal thyroid function test results, and a negative virology screen, including both polymerase chain reaction and IgM tests for herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2, varicella-zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus.
case_info.caption: Nodular vegetating lesions on the chin, lower lip, and right nasal ala (A), and papulovesicular lesions on the left hemiface (B).
case_info.explanation: Cutaneous biopsies of the vegetating lesion on the lip and 1 of the hand lesions showed a dense neutrophilic infiltrate on the reticular dermis with multiple foci of vasculitis, including marked fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls (Figure 2A). Multiple round mononucleated cells with an optically empty peripheral perinuclear halo were also identified (Figure 2B). Immunohistochemistry findings revealed diffuse positivity for myeloperoxidase that spared the round cells, which positive for the histiocytic marker CD163 and, focally, for CD3; CD20 was negative. Results of Ziehl-Neelsen and periodic acid–Schiff stains ruled out the presence of microorganisms. Clinical and pathological findings were in keeping with iododerma. The diagnosis was corroborated by a markedly raised serum iodine level (19 992 μg/L [normal range, 45-100 μg/L]). Complete resolution of skin lesions was possible with a combination of topical fusidic acid with betamethasone and oral corticosteroid 0.5 mg/kg/d tapered over 1 month. The patient’s fatigue and malaise also considerably improved. Iododerma is a rare type of halogenoderma that develops after exposure to iodine-containing compounds (eg, oral and intravenous iodinated contrast dyes, potassium iodide, amiodarone, topical wound care products). It mainly affects patients with kidney disease owing to impaired renal clearance and accumulation of iodine in the bloodstream.1,2Generally, it takes months of continuous exposure to a halogen (eg, oral iodine) to develop a halogenoderma. However, in the context of intravenous administration, cutaneous lesions can appear within 2 to 3 days (ranging from several hours to 8 days), especially in the context of kidney failure.1-3 Iododerma can present a diagnostic challenge. Clinically, lesions can progress rapidly and be polymorphous. However, the most common presentations are acneiform pustular eruptions1and vegetative plaques.2,4In extreme cases, patients can experience toxic effects and present with multiorgan involvement.2 Pathologically, a neutrophil-predominant inflammatory infiltrate is fairly unspecific and can be found in neutrophilic dermatoses such as Sweet syndrome and some infectious diseases.5In the present case, we also found histologic features that had recently been described in iododerma, namely a neutrophilic dermatosis with vasculitis and haloed structures simulatingCryptococcus.2Similarly to the 3 cases previously reported by Ko et al,5we showed that these cryptococcal-like structures were positive for a histiocytic marker and negative for myeloperoxidase. These structures in the setting of neutrophilic dermatosis should also be recognized as part of the histologic spectrum of iododerma. Knowledge of this histologic mimicker is important not only to facilitate the diagnosis, but also to avoid unnecessary antifungal medications.6 Pemphigus vegetans is a rare variant of pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid blisters that become erosions and can form fungoid vegetations in intertriginous areas, the face, and scalp. The characteristic tongue involvement and the presence of suprabasal acantholysis with positive immunofluorescence are distinct aspects.7Pyostomatitis vegetans is characterized by oral involvement with classic snail-track erosions, a strong association with inflammatory bowel disease, peripheral eosinophilia, and characteristic histological features (eg, intraepithelial abscesses with large amount of eosinophils).8Superficial granulomatous pyoderma is a rare variant of pyoderma gangrenosum with a more indolent course. However, facial involvement is particularly uncommon. A characteristic 3-layered granuloma is seen on histological findings.9 With the present case we want to highlight that, despite the diagnostic challenges, a history of exposure to iodine in the context of kidney disease with acute acneiform and/or vegetating lesions should raise the suspicion of iododerma. The diagnosis can be reiterated by histological findings of neutrophilic dermatosis with cryptococcal-like structures (with or without vasculitis), and confirmed by high serum or urine iodine levels. The main treatment of iododerma is to remove the trigger. In some cases, no additional therapy is required. In the case reported, the lesions healed completely with use of systemic corticosteroids, but cyclosporine and hemodialysis are possible alternatives.4

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s undergoing peritoneal dialysis for kidney failure who was also being investigated for severe hyperparathyroidism presented with multiple skin lesions 1 day after undergoing cervical computed tomography with iodinated contrast. Physical examination revealed a polymorphous cutaneous eruption characterized by nodular vegetating lesions on the lower lip and right nasal ala (Figure 1A); papulovesicular lesions, either umbilicated or with an erosive center, clustered on the left cheek (Figure 1B); and 2 papulovesicular lesions with an erythematous-to-violaceous halo at the cannula insertion sites on the back of the right hand and the inner side of the wrist. The patient reported that the lesions were painful, with the ones in the oral mucosa impairing feeding. Additional symptoms included fever, fatigue, rhinorrhea, and odynophagia. Investigations revealed a negative COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction test, mildly raised inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 24.2 mg/dL), normal thyroid function test results, and a negative virology screen, including both polymerase chain reaction and IgM tests for herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2, varicella-zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus.
case_info.caption: Nodular vegetating lesions on the chin, lower lip, and right nasal ala (A), and papulovesicular lesions on the left hemiface (B).
case_info.explanation: Cutaneous biopsies of the vegetating lesion on the lip and 1 of the hand lesions showed a dense neutrophilic infiltrate on the reticular dermis with multiple foci of vasculitis, including marked fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls (Figure 2A). Multiple round mononucleated cells with an optically empty peripheral perinuclear halo were also identified (Figure 2B). Immunohistochemistry findings revealed diffuse positivity for myeloperoxidase that spared the round cells, which positive for the histiocytic marker CD163 and, focally, for CD3; CD20 was negative. Results of Ziehl-Neelsen and periodic acid–Schiff stains ruled out the presence of microorganisms. Clinical and pathological findings were in keeping with iododerma. The diagnosis was corroborated by a markedly raised serum iodine level (19 992 μg/L [normal range, 45-100 μg/L]). Complete resolution of skin lesions was possible with a combination of topical fusidic acid with betamethasone and oral corticosteroid 0.5 mg/kg/d tapered over 1 month. The patient’s fatigue and malaise also considerably improved. Iododerma is a rare type of halogenoderma that develops after exposure to iodine-containing compounds (eg, oral and intravenous iodinated contrast dyes, potassium iodide, amiodarone, topical wound care products). It mainly affects patients with kidney disease owing to impaired renal clearance and accumulation of iodine in the bloodstream.1,2Generally, it takes months of continuous exposure to a halogen (eg, oral iodine) to develop a halogenoderma. However, in the context of intravenous administration, cutaneous lesions can appear within 2 to 3 days (ranging from several hours to 8 days), especially in the context of kidney failure.1-3 Iododerma can present a diagnostic challenge. Clinically, lesions can progress rapidly and be polymorphous. However, the most common presentations are acneiform pustular eruptions1and vegetative plaques.2,4In extreme cases, patients can experience toxic effects and present with multiorgan involvement.2 Pathologically, a neutrophil-predominant inflammatory infiltrate is fairly unspecific and can be found in neutrophilic dermatoses such as Sweet syndrome and some infectious diseases.5In the present case, we also found histologic features that had recently been described in iododerma, namely a neutrophilic dermatosis with vasculitis and haloed structures simulatingCryptococcus.2Similarly to the 3 cases previously reported by Ko et al,5we showed that these cryptococcal-like structures were positive for a histiocytic marker and negative for myeloperoxidase. These structures in the setting of neutrophilic dermatosis should also be recognized as part of the histologic spectrum of iododerma. Knowledge of this histologic mimicker is important not only to facilitate the diagnosis, but also to avoid unnecessary antifungal medications.6 Pemphigus vegetans is a rare variant of pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid blisters that become erosions and can form fungoid vegetations in intertriginous areas, the face, and scalp. The characteristic tongue involvement and the presence of suprabasal acantholysis with positive immunofluorescence are distinct aspects.7Pyostomatitis vegetans is characterized by oral involvement with classic snail-track erosions, a strong association with inflammatory bowel disease, peripheral eosinophilia, and characteristic histological features (eg, intraepithelial abscesses with large amount of eosinophils).8Superficial granulomatous pyoderma is a rare variant of pyoderma gangrenosum with a more indolent course. However, facial involvement is particularly uncommon. A characteristic 3-layered granuloma is seen on histological findings.9 With the present case we want to highlight that, despite the diagnostic challenges, a history of exposure to iodine in the context of kidney disease with acute acneiform and/or vegetating lesions should raise the suspicion of iododerma. The diagnosis can be reiterated by histological findings of neutrophilic dermatosis with cryptococcal-like structures (with or without vasculitis), and confirmed by high serum or urine iodine levels. The main treatment of iododerma is to remove the trigger. In some cases, no additional therapy is required. In the case reported, the lesions healed completely with use of systemic corticosteroids, but cyclosporine and hemodialysis are possible alternatives.4

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s undergoing peritoneal dialysis for kidney failure who was also being investigated for severe hyperparathyroidism presented with multiple skin lesions 1 day after undergoing cervical computed tomography with iodinated contrast. Physical examination revealed a polymorphous cutaneous eruption characterized by nodular vegetating lesions on the lower lip and right nasal ala (Figure 1A); papulovesicular lesions, either umbilicated or with an erosive center, clustered on the left cheek (Figure 1B); and 2 papulovesicular lesions with an erythematous-to-violaceous halo at the cannula insertion sites on the back of the right hand and the inner side of the wrist. The patient reported that the lesions were painful, with the ones in the oral mucosa impairing feeding. Additional symptoms included fever, fatigue, rhinorrhea, and odynophagia. Investigations revealed a negative COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction test, mildly raised inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 24.2 mg/dL), normal thyroid function test results, and a negative virology screen, including both polymerase chain reaction and IgM tests for herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2, varicella-zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus.
case_info.caption: Nodular vegetating lesions on the chin, lower lip, and right nasal ala (A), and papulovesicular lesions on the left hemiface (B).
case_info.explanation: Cutaneous biopsies of the vegetating lesion on the lip and 1 of the hand lesions showed a dense neutrophilic infiltrate on the reticular dermis with multiple foci of vasculitis, including marked fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls (Figure 2A). Multiple round mononucleated cells with an optically empty peripheral perinuclear halo were also identified (Figure 2B). Immunohistochemistry findings revealed diffuse positivity for myeloperoxidase that spared the round cells, which positive for the histiocytic marker CD163 and, focally, for CD3; CD20 was negative. Results of Ziehl-Neelsen and periodic acid–Schiff stains ruled out the presence of microorganisms. Clinical and pathological findings were in keeping with iododerma. The diagnosis was corroborated by a markedly raised serum iodine level (19 992 μg/L [normal range, 45-100 μg/L]). Complete resolution of skin lesions was possible with a combination of topical fusidic acid with betamethasone and oral corticosteroid 0.5 mg/kg/d tapered over 1 month. The patient’s fatigue and malaise also considerably improved. Iododerma is a rare type of halogenoderma that develops after exposure to iodine-containing compounds (eg, oral and intravenous iodinated contrast dyes, potassium iodide, amiodarone, topical wound care products). It mainly affects patients with kidney disease owing to impaired renal clearance and accumulation of iodine in the bloodstream.1,2Generally, it takes months of continuous exposure to a halogen (eg, oral iodine) to develop a halogenoderma. However, in the context of intravenous administration, cutaneous lesions can appear within 2 to 3 days (ranging from several hours to 8 days), especially in the context of kidney failure.1-3 Iododerma can present a diagnostic challenge. Clinically, lesions can progress rapidly and be polymorphous. However, the most common presentations are acneiform pustular eruptions1and vegetative plaques.2,4In extreme cases, patients can experience toxic effects and present with multiorgan involvement.2 Pathologically, a neutrophil-predominant inflammatory infiltrate is fairly unspecific and can be found in neutrophilic dermatoses such as Sweet syndrome and some infectious diseases.5In the present case, we also found histologic features that had recently been described in iododerma, namely a neutrophilic dermatosis with vasculitis and haloed structures simulatingCryptococcus.2Similarly to the 3 cases previously reported by Ko et al,5we showed that these cryptococcal-like structures were positive for a histiocytic marker and negative for myeloperoxidase. These structures in the setting of neutrophilic dermatosis should also be recognized as part of the histologic spectrum of iododerma. Knowledge of this histologic mimicker is important not only to facilitate the diagnosis, but also to avoid unnecessary antifungal medications.6 Pemphigus vegetans is a rare variant of pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid blisters that become erosions and can form fungoid vegetations in intertriginous areas, the face, and scalp. The characteristic tongue involvement and the presence of suprabasal acantholysis with positive immunofluorescence are distinct aspects.7Pyostomatitis vegetans is characterized by oral involvement with classic snail-track erosions, a strong association with inflammatory bowel disease, peripheral eosinophilia, and characteristic histological features (eg, intraepithelial abscesses with large amount of eosinophils).8Superficial granulomatous pyoderma is a rare variant of pyoderma gangrenosum with a more indolent course. However, facial involvement is particularly uncommon. A characteristic 3-layered granuloma is seen on histological findings.9 With the present case we want to highlight that, despite the diagnostic challenges, a history of exposure to iodine in the context of kidney disease with acute acneiform and/or vegetating lesions should raise the suspicion of iododerma. The diagnosis can be reiterated by histological findings of neutrophilic dermatosis with cryptococcal-like structures (with or without vasculitis), and confirmed by high serum or urine iodine levels. The main treatment of iododerma is to remove the trigger. In some cases, no additional therapy is required. case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s undergoing peritoneal dialysis for kidney failure who was also being investigated for severe hyperparathyroidism presented with multiple skin lesions 1 day after undergoing cervical computed tomography with iodinated contrast. Physical examination revealed a polymorphous cutaneous eruption characterized by nodular vegetating lesions on the lower lip and right nasal ala (Figure 1A); papulovesicular lesions, either umbilicated or with an erosive center, clustered on the left cheek (Figure 1B); and 2 papulovesicular lesions with an erythematous-to-violaceous halo at the cannula insertion sites on the back of the right hand and the inner side of the wrist. The patient reported that the lesions were painful, with the ones in the oral mucosa impairing feeding. Additional symptoms included fever, fatigue, rhinorrhea, and odynophagia. Investigations revealed a negative COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction test, mildly raised inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 24.2 mg/dL), normal thyroid function test results, and a negative virology screen, including both polymerase chain reaction and IgM tests for herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2, varicella-zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus.
case_info.caption: Nodular vegetating lesions on the chin, lower lip, and right nasal ala (A), and papulovesicular lesions on the left hemiface (B).
case_info.explanation: Cutaneous biopsies of the vegetating lesion on the lip and 1 of the hand lesions showed a dense neutrophilic infiltrate on the reticular dermis with multiple foci of vasculitis, including marked fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls (Figure 2A). Multiple round mononucleated cells with an optically empty peripheral perinuclear halo were also identified (Figure 2B). Immunohistochemistry findings revealed diffuse positivity for myeloperoxidase that spared the round cells, which positive for the histiocytic marker CD163 and, focally, for CD3; CD20 was negative. Results of Ziehl-Neelsen and periodic acid–Schiff stains ruled out the presence of microorganisms. Clinical and pathological findings were in keeping with iododerma. The diagnosis was corroborated by a markedly raised serum iodine level (19 992 μg/L [normal range, 45-100 μg/L]). Complete resolution of skin lesions was possible with a combination of topical fusidic acid with betamethasone and oral corticosteroid 0.5 mg/kg/d tapered over 1 month. The patient’s fatigue and malaise also considerably improved. Iododerma is a rare type of halogenoderma that develops after exposure to iodine-containing compounds (eg, oral and intravenous iodinated contrast dyes, potassium iodide, amiodarone, topical wound care products). It mainly affects patients with kidney disease owing to impaired renal clearance and accumulation of iodine in the bloodstream.1,2Generally, it takes months of continuous exposure to a halogen (eg, oral iodine) to develop a halogenoderma. However, in the context of intravenous administration, cutaneous lesions can appear within 2 to 3 days (ranging from several hours to 8 days), especially in the context of kidney failure.1-3 Iododerma can present a diagnostic challenge. Clinically, lesions can progress rapidly and be polymorphous. However, the most common presentations are acneiform pustular eruptions1and vegetative plaques.2,4In extreme cases, patients can experience toxic effects and present with multiorgan involvement.2 Pathologically, a neutrophil-predominant inflammatory infiltrate is fairly unspecific and can be found in neutrophilic dermatoses such as Sweet syndrome and some infectious diseases.5In the present case, we also found histologic features that had recently been described in iododerma, namely a neutrophilic dermatosis with vasculitis and haloed structures simulatingCryptococcus.2Similarly to the 3 cases previously reported by Ko et al,5we showed that these cryptococcal-like structures were positive for a histiocytic marker and negative for myeloperoxidase. These structures in the setting of neutrophilic dermatosis should also be recognized as part of the histologic spectrum of iododerma. Knowledge of this histologic mimicker is important not only to facilitate the diagnosis, but also to avoid unnecessary antifungal medications.6 Pemphigus vegetans is a rare variant of pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid blisters that become erosions and can form fungoid vegetations in intertriginous areas, the face, and scalp. The characteristic tongue involvement and the presence of suprabasal acantholysis with positive immunofluorescence are distinct aspects.7Pyostomatitis vegetans is characterized by oral involvement with classic snail-track erosions, a strong association with inflammatory bowel disease, peripheral eosinophilia, and characteristic histological features (eg, intraepithelial abscesses with large amount of eosinophils).8Superficial granulomatous pyoderma is a rare variant of pyoderma gangrenosum with a more indolent course. However, facial involvement is particularly uncommon. A characteristic 3-layered granuloma is seen on histological findings.9 With the present case we want to highlight that, despite the diagnostic challenges, a history of exposure to iodine in the context of kidney disease with acute acneiform and/or vegetating lesions should raise the suspicion of iododerma. The diagnosis can be reiterated by histological findings of neutrophilic dermatosis with cryptococcal-like structures (with or without vasculitis), and confirmed by high serum or urine iodine levels. The main treatment of iododerma is to remove the trigger. In some cases, no additional therapy is required. In the case reported, the lesions healed completely with use of systemic corticosteroids, but cyclosporine and hemodialysis are possible alternatives.4

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s undergoing peritoneal dialysis for kidney failure who was also being investigated for severe hyperparathyroidism presented with multiple skin lesions 1 day after undergoing cervical computed tomography with iodinated contrast. Physical examination revealed a polymorphous cutaneous eruption characterized by nodular vegetating lesions on the lower lip and right nasal ala (Figure 1A); papulovesicular lesions, either umbilicated or with an erosive center, clustered on the left cheek (Figure 1B); and 2 papulovesicular lesions with an erythematous-to-violaceous halo at the cannula insertion sites on the back of the right hand and the inner side of the wrist. The patient reported that the lesions were painful, with the ones in the oral mucosa impairing feeding. Additional symptoms included fever, fatigue, rhinorrhea, and odynophagia. Investigations revealed a negative COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction test, mildly raised inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 24.2 mg/dL), normal thyroid function test results, and a negative virology screen, including both polymerase chain reaction and IgM tests for herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2, varicella-zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus.
case_info.caption: Nodular vegetating lesions on the chin, lower lip, and right nasal ala (A), and papulovesicular lesions on the left hemiface (B).
case_info.explanation: Cutaneous biopsies of the vegetating lesion on the lip and 1 of the hand lesions showed a dense neutrophilic infiltrate on the reticular dermis with multiple foci of vasculitis, including marked fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls (Figure 2A). Multiple round mononucleated cells with an optically empty peripheral perinuclear halo were also identified (Figure 2B). Immunohistochemistry findings revealed diffuse positivity for myeloperoxidase that spared the round cells, which positive for the histiocytic marker CD163 and, focally, for CD3; CD20 was negative. Results of Ziehl-Neelsen and periodic acid–Schiff stains ruled out the presence of microorganisms. Clinical and pathological findings were in keeping with iododerma. The diagnosis was corroborated by a markedly raised serum iodine level (19 992 μg/L [normal range, 45-100 μg/L]). Complete resolution of skin lesions was possible with a combination of topical fusidic acid with betamethasone and oral corticosteroid 0.5 mg/kg/d tapered over 1 month. The patient’s fatigue and malaise also considerably improved. Iododerma is a rare type of halogenoderma that develops after exposure to iodine-containing compounds (eg, oral and intravenous iodinated contrast dyes, potassium iodide, amiodarone, topical wound care products). It mainly affects patients with kidney disease owing to impaired renal clearance and accumulation of iodine in the bloodstream.1,2Generally, it takes months of continuous exposure to a halogen (eg, oral iodine) to develop a halogenoderma. However, in the context of intravenous administration, cutaneous lesions can appear within 2 to 3 days (ranging from several hours to 8 days), especially in the context of kidney failure.1-3 Iododerma can present a diagnostic challenge. Clinically, lesions can progress rapidly and be polymorphous. However, the most common presentations are acneiform pustular eruptions1and vegetative plaques.2,4In extreme cases, patients can experience toxic effects and present with multiorgan involvement.2 Pathologically, a neutrophil-predominant inflammatory infiltrate is fairly unspecific and can be found in neutrophilic dermatoses such as Sweet syndrome and some infectious diseases.5In the present case, we also found histologic features that had recently been described in iododerma, namely a neutrophilic dermatosis with vasculitis and haloed structures simulatingCryptococcus.2Similarly to the 3 cases previously reported by Ko et al,5we showed that these cryptococcal-like structures were positive for a histiocytic marker and negative for myeloperoxidase. These structures in the setting of neutrophilic dermatosis should also be recognized as part of the histologic spectrum of iododerma. Knowledge of this histologic mimicker is important not only to facilitate the diagnosis, but also to avoid unnecessary antifungal medications.6 Pemphigus vegetans is a rare variant of pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid blisters that become erosions and can form fungoid vegetations in intertriginous areas, the face, and scalp. The characteristic tongue involvement and the presence of suprabasal acantholysis with positive immunofluorescence are distinct aspects.7Pyostomatitis vegetans is characterized by oral involvement with classic snail-track erosions, a strong association with inflammatory bowel disease, peripheral eosinophilia, and characteristic histological features (eg, intraepithelial abscesses with large amount of eosinophils).8Superficial granulomatous pyoderma is a rare variant of pyoderma gangrenosum with a more indolent course. However, facial involvement is particularly uncommon. A characteristic 3-layered granuloma is seen on histological findings.9 With the present case we want to highlight that, despite the diagnostic challenges, a history of exposure to iodine in the context of kidney disease with acute acneiform and/or vegetating lesions should raise the suspicion of iododerma. The diagnosis can be reiterated by histological findings of neutrophilic dermatosis with cryptococcal-like structures (with or without vasculitis), and confirmed by high serum or urine iodine levels. The main treatment of iododerma is to remove the trigger. In some cases, no additional therapy is required. In the case reported, the lesions healed completely with use of systemic corticosteroids, but cyclosporine and hemodialysis are possible alternatives.4

[Case]
A woman in her 30s undergoing peritoneal dialysis for kidney failure who was also being investigated for severe hyperparathyroidism presented with multiple skin lesions 1 day after undergoing cervical computed tomography with iodinated contrast. Physical examination revealed a polymorphous cutaneous eruption characterized by nodular vegetating lesions on the lower lip and right nasal ala (Figure 1A); papulovesicular lesions, either umbilicated or with an erosive center, clustered on the left cheek (Figure 1B); and 2 papulovesicular lesions with an erythematous-to-violaceous halo at the cannula insertion sites on the back of the right hand and the inner side of the wrist. The patient reported that the lesions were painful, with the ones in the oral mucosa impairing feeding. Additional symptoms included fever, fatigue, rhinorrhea, and odynophagia. Investigations revealed a negative COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction test, mildly raised inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, 24.2 mg/dL), normal thyroid function test results, and a negative virology screen, including both polymerase chain reaction and IgM tests for herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2, varicella-zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus.

You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.
